pages.title: INTRODUCTION
pages.html:
INTRODUCTION

Before You Read This Book

You are in more high-stakes conversations than almost any professional alive.

Every showing is a conversation. Every offer is a conversation. Every negotiation, every listing appointment, every time a buyer says "we need to think about it" — that is a conversation with a score attached to it. That score is moving whether you are tracking it or not.

Most agents lose deals they should have won. Not because they said the wrong thing. Because they were hearing words when they should have been watching the score.

This book teaches you to watch the score.

◆

The PLT Framework identifies three scores running simultaneously in every conversation:

PROFIT — who controls the frame. Who has leverage. Who is closer to getting what they want.

LOVE — the relationship account. Trust, credibility, loyalty. The thing that takes months to build and one sentence to burn.

TAX — what the conversation is costing. Risk, exposure, obligation. What each person will owe because of what was said.

Every line in every conversation moves all three. The agent who can see those movements in real time — in the showing, in the negotiation, in the kitchen conversation before the offer gets written — that agent closes differently. Holds the room differently. Keeps clients longer. Wins listing appointments they would have lost.

That is what The Scorer teaches.

◆

This book does not require you to have read anything else. It starts from zero and ends with a complete tool you can carry into any conversation in the transaction.

The characters in this book are the people you work with every day:

The Buyer. The Seller. The Agent. The Loan Officer. The BDM. The Family.

Every conversation is between them. Every score is real. Every lesson is from the transaction itself.

By the last page you will not hear conversations the same way again.

pages.title: PART ONE
pages.html:
PART ONE

The World

pages.title: CHAPTER 1
pages.html:
CHAPTER 1

The Transaction Nobody Sees

A real estate transaction is not a property exchange.

It looks like a property exchange from the outside. There is a house. There is a buyer. There is a price. There is a closing date. Those things are real. But underneath them, running simultaneously, is a web of scored conversations between six types of people — and the outcome of the transaction is determined by those conversations, not by the property.

The house does not close because it was priced correctly. It closes because the conversations that surrounded the pricing, the offer, the inspection, and the final walkthrough all moved the right scores in the right directions.

The deal falls apart — and it almost always falls apart for the same reason — because someone let a score drain without noticing. The buyer went cold. The seller got defensive. The agent lost the room. The loan officer killed the confidence. Someone let the Love account hit zero and nobody saw it happening.

◆

Here is the transaction as it actually exists:

The Buyer is the most emotionally exposed person in the room. They are spending the most money they have ever spent on something they cannot fully evaluate in the time they have to decide. They are running fear, hope, excitement, and doubt simultaneously. Every line they say is driven by all four.

The Seller has an asset they have lived in, built equity in, and attached meaning to. They distrust everyone who wants to take something from them. Their opening position is almost always emotionally inflated. Their real number and their stated number are rarely the same.

The Agent is the professional who reads people for a living — but most agents read the wrong things. They read enthusiasm instead of commitment. They read objections as obstacles instead of information. They focus on closing when they should be scoring.

The Loan Officer holds the deal together or kills it with a single phone call. They run the highest-Tax conversations in the transaction. What they say about risk and qualification shapes the buyer's entire financial confidence in the room.

The BDM is the person behind the agent — building relationships, managing pipelines, creating the conditions for deals before deals exist. The BDM's conversations almost never involve the property at all. They are pure Profit and Love transactions.

The Family is every person who is not in the conversation officially but is in every conversation actually. The spouse who hasn't seen the house but has a feeling. The mother who calls after the showing. The partner who asks what the monthly payment actually is at 10pm when the agent is not in the room.

◆

Those six people are running scores against each other across the entire transaction. Some of those scores they know about. Most of them they don't.

The Scorer knows about all of them.

pages.title: CHAPTER 2
pages.html:
CHAPTER 2

Why Deals Fall Apart

Every deal that falls apart falls apart for one of three reasons.

The Profit collapsed. Someone lost the frame. The buyer started negotiating against themselves. The seller dug into a position they couldn't exit without losing face. The agent stopped being the expert and started being the pleader. When Profit collapses in a real estate transaction the deal doesn't always die immediately — it gets fragile. It requires everything else to go right. And everything rarely goes right in a fragile deal.

The Love burned. Trust broke. The buyer felt manipulated by the agent. The seller felt disrespected by the offer. The loan officer delivered bad news in a way that felt like an accusation. Love does not burn with a fire — it burns with a silence. The buyer who stops asking questions. The seller who goes short in their responses. The client who says "let me think about it" and doesn't call back. That's the Love account hitting empty.

The Tax became unbearable. The risk exceeded the desire. The buyer looked at the inspection report and decided the exposure was too high. The seller looked at the net sheet and decided the cost of selling was not worth the freedom. The Tax didn't have to be real — it had to feel real. And the agent who can't manage how Tax feels in the room will lose deals to inspections, appraisals, and closing costs that should never have ended a transaction.

◆

The agent who can score conversations in real time sees these three collapses coming before they happen. Not because they have a crystal ball. Because every collapse is preceded by a series of small score movements that are visible if you know what to watch.

The Profit starts slipping three conversations before the buyer stops committing. The Love starts burning two sentences before the seller gets defensive. The Tax becomes unbearable one line before the client says "let me think about it."

The scorer sees those movements. The scorer acts before the collapse.

pages.title: PART TWO
pages.html:
PART TWO

Profit. Love. Tax.

pages.title: CHAPTER 3
pages.html:
CHAPTER 3

Profit

Profit is leverage.

Not money. Not commission. Not the sale price. Leverage — who controls the frame of the conversation. Who has the information advantage. Who is closer to getting what they actually want. Who set the terms that everyone else is responding to.

In a showing, the agent who walks in having already researched the buyer's search history, knows their approval amount, and understands the three things that will make or break the decision for this specific buyer — that agent has Profit before they open the door.

The agent who walks in hoping the house sells itself has none.

◆

Profit moves on information. On positioning. On who controls the narrative.

Watch for the frame move. The person who names the category first controls it.

"This is a starter home" — the agent just set the buyer's expectation ceiling.

"This is a transition property" — the agent just reframed the same house as temporary.

"This is the best value in the zip code right now" — the agent just made the conversation about the market instead of the property.

Three different sentences. Three different Profit positions. Same house.

◆

Profit also moves on patience. The first person to show their full hand loses Profit. In a negotiation, the buyer who says "we really love this house" has just handed three Profit points to the seller's agent. The seller who calls to check on the offer before the deadline has done the same.

Patience is not silence. Patience is the discipline to let the other side move first.

The scorer watches Profit for: who is asking questions vs. who is answering them. Who named the number first. Who is explaining their position. Who is waiting.

The person doing more explaining is usually losing Profit.

pages.title: CHAPTER 4
pages.html:
CHAPTER 4

Love

Love is the relationship account.

It is built slowly and spent in seconds. It is the reason a client takes your call on a Sunday when three other agents have their number. It is the reason a seller accepts a slightly lower offer from a buyer whose agent they trust. It is the reason a loan officer who has worked with you for two years goes the extra mile on a difficult file.

Love is not likeability. This is the most common mistake agents make. They confuse being liked with having Love capital. A client can like you and not trust you. Likeability is surface. Love runs deeper — it is the accumulated record of whether you have been honest, reliable, and genuinely on their side when it would have been easier to be on your own.

◆

Love moves on honesty more than any other signal.

The agent who tells a buyer "this house has a problem I want you to understand before you fall in love with it" — that agent just built Love. Not because they delivered bad news. Because they delivered it before they had to, before it became a surprise, before it cost the buyer something.

The agent who waits for the inspection to surface that problem because they were afraid of losing the sale — that agent spent Love they didn't know they had.

◆

Watch for Love burning in real time:

The buyer who stops making eye contact with the agent during the showing.

The seller who answers in one sentence when they used to talk for five.

The client who says "yeah, okay" instead of asking a follow-up question.

The loan officer who stopped being called by first name.

These are not personality shifts. They are score movements. The Love account is draining. The scorer sees it and acts — not with a pitch, not with energy, with honesty. Love can only be rebuilt the same way it was built: one honest interaction at a time.

pages.title: CHAPTER 5
pages.html:
CHAPTER 5

Tax

Tax is what the conversation costs.

Not what it costs in dollars, though dollars are often the visible form of it. Tax is the risk being transferred, the obligation being created, the exposure being accepted. Tax is what you will owe because of what was said — and that debt does not always come due at closing. Sometimes it comes due six months later when the client calls with a problem they didn't anticipate and they expect you to solve it.

In real estate, Tax runs in both directions simultaneously.

Every conversation transfers some Tax from one party to another. The agent who says "don't worry, this is standard" has just accepted Tax — the buyer now holds them responsible for whatever "standard" means if it turns out to be a problem. The loan officer who says "you're well-qualified" has just transferred Tax to themselves — the client will hold them accountable to that statement if the file runs into trouble.

◆

High-Tax conversations are the ones most agents avoid. The inspection conversation. The appraisal gap conversation. The conversation about what happens if the financing falls through. Agents avoid them because they feel like they are creating problems by naming them.

The scorer knows the opposite is true.

Named Tax is manageable. Unnamed Tax compounds until it becomes a crisis. The agent who walks the buyer through every possible cost before the offer — inspection issues, closing costs, potential appraisal gaps — has just done two things simultaneously. They have managed the Tax before it lands as a surprise, and they have built massive Love by demonstrating that they are the kind of agent who tells clients the full truth.

Low Profit, high Love, managed Tax. That is the safest position to be in on the back half of a transaction.

◆

Watch Tax for: the agent who is promising things they cannot control. The loan officer using qualifiers like "probably" and "should be fine" — those are Tax building quietly in the background. The buyer who keeps asking about things that weren't in the disclosure. The seller who adds conditions to the contract after it's been signed.

Every qualifier is a Tax signal. Somebody is protecting themselves from something they can see that they are not saying out loud.

pages.title: CHAPTER 6
pages.html:
CHAPTER 6

Intent. Body. Pressure.

The three scores — Profit, Love, Tax — are moved by three signals.

You do not need to know what someone is thinking to score their move. You need to read three things:

◆

Intent — What they actually want from this line.

Not what the words say. What the words are for. The buyer who says "we're just looking" is not just looking. Their Intent is to reduce the pressure of the showing so they can evaluate without committing. The seller who says "we're not in a hurry" is not telling you about their timeline. Their Intent is to protect Profit by signaling that your urgency cannot be used against them.

Intent is always about position. What position is this person trying to establish with this line? Read the position, not the words.

◆

Body — What their physical presence is telling you.

The buyer who slows down in the kitchen is giving you information their mouth hasn't provided yet. The seller who crosses their arms when the price is mentioned is telling you the number triggered something. The loan officer who pauses before answering a question about timeline is calculating something they haven't said.

Body is not about reading microexpressions. It is about reading pace and energy. Does the room feel faster or slower after that line? Is the person leaning in or creating distance? Is the energy building or draining?

The room's energy always moves before the words confirm it.

◆

Pressure — What external force is acting on this conversation.

The buyer who saw another offer come in this morning is under different Pressure than the buyer who is the only offer. The seller who has already bought their next house is under different Pressure than the seller who has nowhere to go. The agent whose quarter is ending is under different Pressure than the agent who closed three deals last week.

Pressure shapes every line in the conversation. The person who appears to be negotiating from logic is almost always negotiating from Pressure. Find the Pressure and you find the real position.

◆

Intent. Body. Pressure. Read all three on every line. Then score the move.

The scorer is not slower than the conversation. The scorer is inside the conversation seeing it at a level the other person is not operating on.

pages.title: PART THREE
pages.html:
PART THREE

The Characters

pages.title: CHAPTER 7
pages.html:
CHAPTER 7

The Buyer

The Buyer is the most emotionally exposed person in the transaction.

They are spending the largest sum of money they have ever committed to in the shortest decision window they have ever been given. They have done research that gave them the illusion of knowledge but not the reality of it. They have looked at Zillow. They have read articles. They have watched YouTube videos about what to look for in a foundation. None of it prepared them for standing in a kitchen they love and being asked to decide on it by Thursday.

The Buyer's Profit position is almost always weaker than they believe it is. They think their research gave them leverage. It gave them vocabulary. Vocabulary and leverage are not the same thing.

◆

What the Buyer actually wants: certainty that they are not making a mistake.

Everything else — the price, the timeline, the contingencies — is a vehicle for that one thing. The buyer who keeps asking the same question in different forms is not confused about the answer. They are looking for certainty that the answer is the right one.

The agent who understands this stops answering the question and starts building the certainty. Those are not the same move.

◆

pages.title: How to read a Buyer's score:
pages.html:
How to read a Buyer's score:

Profit: Are they asking questions or making statements? Questions mean they are still evaluating. Statements mean they have started deciding. The shift from questions to statements is the Profit signal that commitment is forming.

Love: Are they telling you things they don't need to tell you? Personal details about why they want the house, what the neighborhood means to them, how they imagine the space working. Oversharing is a Love signal. They trust you enough to give you information they have no strategic reason to give.

Tax: Are they asking about problems before there are problems? What if the inspection finds something? What if it doesn't appraise? What if we change our minds? These are Tax questions. The buyer is calculating exposure. The agent who answers these questions honestly before they become urgent has the lowest-Tax client relationship in the transaction.

pages.title: CHAPTER 8
pages.html:
CHAPTER 8

The Seller

The Seller is protecting something.

Not just the price — the price is the number their protection is expressed through. What they are protecting is the meaning the property carries. The years of equity. The improvements they made. The specific memory of the house as the thing they built when everything else was uncertain. The seller is not selling a house. They are quantifying their own story. And they need the number to confirm that the story was worth it.

The agent who prices a seller's home is not just setting a number. They are managing the seller's relationship with their own past. That is why pricing conversations are some of the highest-Tax conversations in the entire transaction.

◆

The Seller's default position is distrust.

Not distrust of the agent specifically — distrust of the transaction. They have heard stories. They know someone who sold and felt they left money on the table. They know someone who used an agent and paid too much in commission for too little in service. They are arriving at this conversation with accumulated skepticism about the category of person sitting across from them.

The agent who leads with credentials feeds that skepticism. The agent who leads with honesty about the market, about the specific challenges of this property, about what the seller should expect — that agent builds Love faster than any other move available.

◆

pages.title: How to read a Seller's score:
pages.html:
How to read a Seller's score:

Profit: Are they citing comps or citing memory? "The Hendersons got 620 for a smaller lot" is a Profit move — they are establishing an anchor. "We spent $40,000 on that kitchen" is a memory move — they are seeking validation, not negotiating. Read the difference.

Love: The first time a seller calls you by first name without prompting, the Love account has moved. The first time they say "what do you think I should do" instead of telling you what they plan to do, the Love account has moved. Small signals. Real movements.

Tax: Every condition a seller adds to the transaction is Tax being shifted back to the buyer. A seller who is piling on conditions is either protecting against a risk they can see or testing how much Tax the buyer will absorb. Find out which.

pages.title: CHAPTER 9
pages.html:
CHAPTER 9

The Agent

The Agent is the only person in the transaction who is in every conversation.

They are in the buyer conversation and the seller conversation and the loan officer conversation and the BDM conversation and, indirectly, in the family conversation when the client goes home and describes what their agent said. The agent's score runs across all of these simultaneously. A Love account burned with a seller at 2pm shows up in the buyer conversation at 5pm because the agent carries it with them.

◆

The Agent's most common scoring error: confusing activity with position.

The agent who calls every day is running high activity. If those calls are providing genuine information — real updates, honest assessments, things the client needs rather than things the agent needs to say — the activity builds Love. If those calls are the agent managing their own anxiety about the deal, the client starts to feel that. Activity without information is Tax. You are spending the client's attention without giving them value in return.

◆

The Agent's score in the transaction runs on three things:

Expertise — do they know more than the client about this market, this property, this process? Expertise is Profit. The agent who does not maintain it loses the frame of every conversation.

Honesty — do they tell the client difficult things early? Honesty is Love. It is the most efficient Love-building tool in the transaction and the most consistently underused.

Patience — do they let the conversation develop or do they push it? Patience is Tax management. The agent who needs the deal to close because their own finances are tight is running the highest-Tax position of anyone in the room.

pages.title: CHAPTER 10
pages.html:
CHAPTER 10

The Loan Officer

The Loan Officer runs the highest-stakes single conversation in the transaction.

Not because the conversation is the most emotional — the offer conversation carries more heat. Not because it involves the most money — the negotiation does. But because the Loan Officer's conversation determines whether everything else proceeds or stops. The approval, the rate, the timeline, the conditions — every piece of the financial architecture is carried in conversations that the Loan Officer controls.

◆

The Loan Officer's most dangerous move: false certainty.

"You're going to be fine." "This is straightforward." "I've done this a hundred times." These are not reassurances. They are Tax being transferred to the Loan Officer that they cannot always carry. The buyer who was told they were going to be fine and then hit an underwriting condition at the two-week mark does not hear "this is a normal part of the process." They hear: you lied to me.

The Loan Officer who says "here are the three things that could affect your timeline and here is exactly what we do if any of them happen" — that Loan Officer has higher Tax in the moment and infinitely more Love over the life of the transaction.

◆

How the Loan Officer's score affects the Agent:

Every time a Loan Officer burns Love with a buyer, the Agent pays part of the bill. The buyer does not fully separate the agent from the loan officer — they are both "my real estate people." The agent who manages the Loan Officer relationship with the same precision they manage the client relationship protects their own score from someone else's mistakes.

pages.title: CHAPTER 11
pages.html:
CHAPTER 11

The BDM

The BDM's job is to make conversations possible that would not otherwise happen.

They are relationship infrastructure. They do not close deals — they create the conditions in which deals become possible. Their conversations are almost never about properties. They are about trust, positioning, mutual benefit, and the slow accumulation of Profit and Love that eventually becomes a referral, a repeat client, a partnership that generates a pipeline.

◆

The BDM scores every conversation as a long-term investment, not a transaction.

A conversation with a builder's representative that produces nothing visible today may produce five listings in eighteen months. A lunch with a corporate relocation coordinator that feels like small talk is actually a Profit accumulation — the BDM is establishing that they are the person who knows the market the way the relocation coordinator needs someone to know it.

The BDM who scores their conversations only by what happened immediately is measuring the wrong thing. Their score runs on months and quarters, not on individual interactions.

◆

The BDM's primary tool is information — specifically, information given freely before it is asked for. The BDM who calls a builder contact to say "I thought you should know the new school district rezoning is going to affect your inventory pricing" before that information is public is doing something specific with their score. They are running a Love move disguised as an information share.

Nobody forgets the person who told them something important before it cost them anything not to know it.

pages.title: CHAPTER 12
pages.html:
CHAPTER 12

The Family

The Family is the most underestimated participant in the transaction.

They are not at the showing. They are not in the negotiation. Their name is not on the offer. But they are in every conversation the buyer or seller has before they go to sleep, and the score that runs in those conversations determines what the client believes when they wake up in the morning.

The agent who wins the client's family wins the deal.

The agent who ignores the family loses deals they do not understand why they lost.

◆

What the Family is running:

The spouse who has not seen the house is running pure Tax. They did not fall in love with the kitchen. They did not feel the neighborhood. They are calculating exposure — financial, logistical, emotional — with no Love to offset it. They are the most skeptical person in the transaction and they have the most influence over the person you are working with.

The agent who finds a way to include the family — not as a formality, but as a genuine participant in the information — converts that pure Tax position into something more balanced. The family member who feels informed does not need to protect against the unknown because they know.

◆

Watch the client's behavior after they talk to family. If the client's questions shift — if they start asking things they weren't asking before — the family has introduced new Tax into the conversation. Find it. Name it. Manage it before it becomes the reason the deal dies.

The question a buyer asks after talking to their mother is almost always the mother's question, not the buyer's. Score it accordingly.

pages.title: PART FOUR
pages.html:
PART FOUR

The Conversations

BUYER / AGENT

The Showing

Marcus has been with his agent, Dana, for six weeks. Three previous showings, no offers. This is the fourth house. The price is at the top of his approved range.

◆

Dana: "I want to tell you something about this house before we go in. The sellers are motivated — they've already bought their next place. That's information the other buyers looking at this don't have."

THE SCORE

PROFIT 74 ▲ 8|LOVE 62 ▲ 6|TAX 28 —

MOVE INTEL SHARE — PROFIT MOVE

Dana just transferred a piece of her Profit to Marcus. She gave him information that improves his negotiating position. This builds Love (she is working for him) and Profit (he now has an anchor for the offer conversation). Tax stays flat because the information creates opportunity, not obligation.

Marcus: "How much motivated are we talking."

THE SCORE

PROFIT 76 ▲ 2|LOVE 62 —|TAX 28 —

MOVE PROBE — SMALL PROFIT GAIN

Marcus is testing the ceiling of the information Dana offered. He did not reveal anything about his own position. He asked a question that forces Dana to either qualify her statement or give him more. Pure Profit accumulation.

Dana: "Motivated enough that if the offer is clean and the timeline works, they might take less than list."

THE SCORE

PROFIT 76 —|LOVE 65 ▲ 3|TAX 30 ▲ 2

MOVE HONEST QUALIFICATION — LOVE BUILD

Dana said "might" — she qualified her statement rather than overselling. That small word is a Love move. It signals that she does not exaggerate to close. Tax increases slightly because Dana has now introduced the possibility of a below-list offer, which creates obligation to advise on offer strategy.

Marcus: "I like the neighborhood. My wife hasn't seen it yet."

THE SCORE

PROFIT 74 ▼ 2|LOVE 65 —|TAX 36 ▲ 6

MOVE FAMILY SIGNAL — TAX ALERT

Marcus just introduced the most important variable in this transaction: his wife has not seen the house. His Profit drops because he has revealed a dependency — the decision cannot be made today. Tax jumps because Dana now has a time and approval problem she did not have thirty seconds ago. The scorer's immediate priority: manage the wife variable before it becomes the reason this deal does not happen.

◆

Dana has a choice at this moment. She can continue the showing and hope Marcus's enthusiasm is contagious enough to carry to his wife. Or she can score the situation correctly and address the wife variable now.

The scorer addresses the variable.

◆

Dana: "Can we get her here this week? If this is the one, I want her to feel it too."

THE SCORE

PROFIT 76 ▲ 2|LOVE 70 ▲ 5|TAX 30 ▼ 6

MOVE FAMILY INCLUSION — LOVE AND PROFIT RECOVERY

Dana just moved three scores simultaneously. Profit recovers because she has taken control of the timeline problem. Love builds because she framed the wife's involvement as something she wants, not something Marcus needs to manage. Tax drops because the unknown (wife's reaction) is now scheduled to become known. This is the highest-value single move available to Dana at this moment in the conversation.

BUYER / LOAN OFFICER

The Pre-Approval Call

Renee is a first-time buyer. Her loan officer, Chris, is on the phone with her three days before she wants to make an offer.

◆

Chris: "So your pre-approval is solid. The income documentation came back clean."

THE SCORE

PROFIT 70 —|LOVE 58 ▲ 4|TAX 22 —

MOVE CONFIRMATION — BASELINE LOVE BUILD

Chris led with good news, which is correct. Love builds because Renee needed confirmation. But Profit and Tax barely moved because the statement was expected — it was not unexpected honesty, just expected delivery. The move was necessary but not powerful.

Renee: "Okay good. So we're all set?"

THE SCORE

PROFIT 70 —|LOVE 58 —|TAX 28 ▲ 6

MOVE PREMATURE CERTAINTY SEEK — TAX BUILD

"Are we all set" is the buyer attempting to close the uncertainty loop. When a buyer asks this question, they are hoping the answer is yes and are not fully prepared for the answer to be anything else. Tax builds because the conversation is now at risk — Chris has to either confirm a certainty he may not have, or manage an expectation he should have managed before this moment.

Chris: "Mostly. There are two conditions on the file I want you to know about before you make the offer. Nothing that should stop the deal but you need to understand them."

THE SCORE

PROFIT 70 —|LOVE 72 ▲ 14|TAX 22 ▼ 6

MOVE HONEST PREVIEW — MAJOR LOVE BUILD

Chris just made the highest-value move available to any Loan Officer in a pre-approval conversation. He said "mostly" instead of "yes" — which is honest. He named the conditions before they became surprises. He framed them correctly ("nothing that should stop the deal"). Love jumps 14 points because this is exactly the conversation Renee needs and almost never gets. Tax drops because the unknown is now named and manageable.

Renee: "What conditions?"

THE SCORE

PROFIT 70 —|LOVE 72 —|TAX 22 —

MOVE ENGAGEMENT — SCORE HOLDS

Renee is asking the right question. The scorer notes that the Love account is stable and the Tax is manageable because Chris created the conditions for this conversation before it became an emergency. The next two minutes will either hold the score or determine the outcome of this transaction.

AGENT / SELLER

The Listing Appointment

Jordan is presenting to the Kellermans. They have lived in the house for eighteen years. Jordan is one of three agents presenting this week.

◆

Mr. Kellerman: "The last agent told us we could get 780."

THE SCORE

PROFIT 62 ▼ 8|LOVE 50 —|TAX 30 ▲ 8

MOVE ANCHOR — PROFIT TRAP

The Kellermans have just deployed the most common listing appointment weapon: a competing anchor. Profit drops for Jordan because she is now in a reactive position — she must either match, beat, or dispute a number that was placed there specifically to control the frame. Tax builds because disputing the anchor creates conflict. Jordan's next move is the most important of the appointment.

Jordan: "I'd be concerned about an agent who told you that before seeing the comps together."

THE SCORE

PROFIT 72 ▲ 10|LOVE 56 ▲ 6|TAX 26 ▼ 4

MOVE FRAME RECLAIM — MAJOR PROFIT RECOVERY

Jordan did not attack the number. She attacked the process that produced the number. This is the correct move. Profit recovers because she has repositioned herself as the agent who uses evidence, not optimism. Love builds because she is implicitly promising the Kellermans that she will not tell them what they want to hear. Tax drops because she has moved the conversation from price competition to process credibility — a much stronger position.

Mr. Kellerman: "She seemed pretty confident."

THE SCORE

PROFIT 72 —|LOVE 56 —|TAX 32 ▲ 6

MOVE PUSHBACK — TAX BUILD

The Kellermans are defending the competing agent. This is emotional attachment to an optimistic number. Tax builds because Jordan must now decide whether to press her position or let it go. Pressing it risks Love. Letting it go surrenders Profit. The scorer reads this as a critical branch in the appointment.

Jordan: "I want you to get the most this house can actually deliver. Let me show you the last six months of sales on your block and you tell me what number you see."

THE SCORE

PROFIT 80 ▲ 8|LOVE 66 ▲ 10|TAX 20 ▼ 12

MOVE EVIDENCE TRANSFER — SCORE DOMINANCE

Jordan moved all three scores simultaneously and in the right direction. Profit climbs because she is taking control of the information. Love climbs because "I want you to get the most" is a client-first framing. Tax drops dramatically because she transferred the pricing decision to the Kellermans — she is not telling them the price, she is asking them to read it themselves. The Kellermans now own the conclusion. This is the highest-value move in a listing appointment.

SELLER / BUYER

The Negotiation

The Patels are selling. The buyer's offer came in at $34,000 under asking. Their agent, Sandra, is walking them through the response.

◆

Mrs. Patel: "That offer is insulting."

THE SCORE

PROFIT 60 —|LOVE 58 —|TAX 38 ▲ 8

MOVE EMOTIONAL ANCHOR — TAX ALERT

The word "insulting" is a Tax signal. Mrs. Patel has framed the offer in emotional terms, which means any counteroffer strategy must navigate her emotional position first. Tax builds because Sandra must now manage a seller whose decision-making framework is dignity-based rather than market-based. These are the hardest negotiations to close.

pages.title: PART FOUR (cont. 2)
pages.html:
Sandra: "I understand that feeling. But I want to tell you what the offer actually says — not what the number looks like, but what the buyer's position actually is."

THE SCORE

PROFIT 64 ▲ 4|LOVE 66 ▲ 8|TAX 28 ▼ 10

MOVE REFRAME — LOVE BUILD, TAX DROP

Sandra acknowledged the emotion without validating the emotional framework. She separated "feeling" from "position." This is precise Love-building — she is with Mrs. Patel emotionally while steering her toward a strategic conversation. Tax drops because she has introduced the possibility of reading the offer differently.

Mrs. Patel: "What do you mean their position?"

THE SCORE

PROFIT 64 —|LOVE 66 —|TAX 28 —

MOVE ENGAGEMENT — SCORE HOLDS

Mrs. Patel asked a question. She is no longer defending — she is listening. This is the shift the scorer waits for. The emotional position has not been abandoned but it has been paused. Sandra now has the room.

Sandra: "They are pre-approved, no contingencies except inspection, and they can close in 21 days. That's an unusually clean offer. The number is low but the structure is what you wanted. A counter at list price with their timeline keeps all of that and moves the conversation forward."

THE SCORE

PROFIT 76 ▲ 12|LOVE 70 ▲ 4|TAX 20 ▼ 8

MOVE ASSET REFRAME — PROFIT DOMINANT MOVE

Sandra has reframed the offer from a price conversation to a structure conversation. Profit climbs because she has given the Patels a counteroffer strategy that does not require them to emotionally accept the original number. Love builds because she is visibly working for their outcome. Tax drops to its lowest point in this conversation because the path forward is clear and executable. This is the move that saves this negotiation.

AGENT / LOAN OFFICER

The Pipeline Call

Devon is an agent. His loan officer, Maria, has been on three of his last four deals. He is calling to discuss a buyer who is 60 days from being ready.

◆

Devon: "I want to get ahead of this one. Marcus is close but not ready. What do I need to tell him to do in the next 60 days to make this clean?"

THE SCORE

PROFIT 74 ▲ 6|LOVE 70 ▲ 4|TAX 18 ▼ 4

MOVE PROACTIVE PLANNING — PROFIT AND LOVE BUILD

Devon is running a move that most agents do not run: he is managing the deal before it is a deal. Profit builds because he is controlling the timeline. Love builds in the Agent/Loan Officer relationship because Maria sees an agent who prepares rather than reacts. Tax drops because the file problems get solved before they become emergencies.

Maria: "Two things. His debt-to-income is borderline — if he can pay down one card it moves him to a cleaner tier. And I'm going to need 60 days of bank statements so tell him no large deposits that aren't documented."

THE SCORE

PROFIT 78 ▲ 4|LOVE 76 ▲ 6|TAX 14 ▼ 4

MOVE SPECIFIC INTELLIGENCE — HIGHEST LOAN OFFICER MOVE

Maria gave Devon specific, actionable information instead of general reassurance. Profit builds because Devon now has a clear preparation strategy. Love between Devon and Maria reaches its highest point in this conversation because she is treating him as a professional partner. Tax drops to near minimum because all the file risk is now identified and manageable before it matters.

Devon: "That's exactly what I needed. I'll handle the client conversation — you'll have a clean file."

THE SCORE

PROFIT 80 ▲ 2|LOVE 78 ▲ 2|TAX 14 —

MOVE COMMITMENT — SCORE LOCKS

Devon made a commitment based on the intelligence Maria provided. Both Profit and Love tick up slightly because he confirmed the partnership dynamic — she provides intelligence, he manages the client, the file arrives clean. This is the Agent/Loan Officer relationship at its most functional.

BUYER / FAMILY

The Kitchen Table

It is 9pm. The Garcias have been to a showing. Elena is telling her mother, Rosa, about the house. Her husband, David, is listening.

◆

Rosa: "How much are they asking?"

THE SCORE

PROFIT 60 ▼ 4|LOVE 62 —|TAX 40 ▲ 10

MOVE PRICE ANCHOR — TAX INTRODUCTION

Rosa's first question is the price. This is the family conversation pattern that agents never see and almost always lose to. Profit drops for the buyer because the price, stated without context, will immediately generate a comparison to something the family member knows — a different property, a different market, a different era. Tax jumps because Rosa now has a number she did not earn through the showing experience.

Elena: "Five-eighty. But Dana says the sellers are motivated and there might be room."

THE SCORE

PROFIT 62 ▲ 2|LOVE 62 —|TAX 38 ▼ 2

MOVE AGENT PROXY — MODERATE RECOVERY

Elena is carrying the agent's Profit into the family conversation. She cited Dana's intelligence. This is a positive signal — it means Dana's Love account with Elena is high enough that Elena is repeating Dana's analysis at her own kitchen table. The scorer notes: this is exactly why building Love with the buyer matters. The agent who the buyer trusts becomes the agent who wins the family conversation by proxy.

Rosa: "Five-eighty is too much. When we bought in '98 you could get a house like that for—"

THE SCORE

PROFIT 54 ▼ 8|LOVE 62 —|TAX 52 ▲ 14

MOVE HISTORICAL ANCHOR — CRITICAL TAX SPIKE

Rosa is comparing 1998 prices to 2024 prices. This is the family conversation that kills more deals than any inspection report. Profit collapses because the buyer's frame has just been contaminated by an irrelevant reference point. Tax spikes to critical levels because Elena will now carry this doubt into tomorrow's conversation with Dana. The scorer's priority: Dana needs to have a family-ready market education conversation with Elena before the next showing.

David: "What did the neighborhood look like?"

THE SCORE

PROFIT 56 ▲ 2|LOVE 64 ▲ 2|TAX 46 ▼ 6

MOVE REDIRECT — SMALL RECOVERY

David shifted the conversation from price to experience. This is an instinctive Love move — he is prioritizing the quality of his wife's experience over the number. Tax drops slightly because the frame has moved from pure financial anxiety to evaluation mode. The scorer notes David as a positive influence and advises Dana to include him deliberately in the process.

BDM / AGENT

The Pipeline Review

Rachel is a BDM. She is in a weekly call with her agent, Tyler, who has had a slow quarter.

◆

Tyler: "I have eight active buyers but nothing is clicking."

THE SCORE

PROFIT 58 —|LOVE 62 —|TAX 34 ▲ 8

MOVE VAGUE COMPLAINT — TAX BUILD

"Nothing is clicking" is not a business analysis. It is a mood expressed as a report. Tax builds because Rachel now must decide whether to validate the complaint or push for specificity. Validating it builds Love but costs Profit. Pushing for specificity builds Profit but risks Love if Tyler reads it as criticism.

Rachel: "Tell me about the three buyers you're most confident in. What's their actual timeline and what's blocking each of them?"

THE SCORE

PROFIT 68 ▲ 10|LOVE 64 ▲ 2|TAX 24 ▼ 10

MOVE DIAGNOSIS DEMAND — MAJOR PROFIT MOVE

Rachel changed the frame from complaint to analysis. Profit builds significantly because she moved the conversation from eight unfocused buyers to three prioritized ones. Love ticks up because the question is not critical — it is constructive. Tax drops because the conversation now has a structure that can produce a decision.

Tyler: "Honestly? Two of them are waiting for rates to come down. The third one — the Garcias — they're ready but the wife's mother keeps questioning the price."

THE SCORE

PROFIT 70 ▲ 2|LOVE 64 —|TAX 20 ▼ 4

MOVE SPECIFIC DIAGNOSIS — CORRECT

Tyler gave Rachel a real answer. Profit ticks up because he moved from vague to specific. The scorer immediately identifies the Garcia situation as the actionable variable: the mother. This is where Rachel's next move should focus.

Rachel: "The Garcia situation is solvable. The mother needs a market conversation, not a property conversation. Can you get Dana to schedule a call that includes the mother? Frame it as a market education session, not a sales call."

THE SCORE

PROFIT 80 ▲ 10|LOVE 70 ▲ 6|TAX 14 ▼ 6

MOVE STRATEGY DELIVERY — DOMINANT MOVE

pages.title: PART FOUR (cont. 3)
pages.html: Rachel diagnosed the specific problem and delivered the specific solution in the same move. Profit builds significantly because the conversation has gone from "nothing is clicking" to a clear executable strategy in four exchanges. Love builds because Tyler now has something to do rather than something to worry about. Tax drops because the path forward is defined.

pages.title: PART FIVE
pages.html:
PART FIVE

The Drills

Score each line before you read the answer. Read the context, read the line, assign Profit/Love/Tax movement, then check your scoring.

The goal is not to match the score exactly. The goal is to train yourself to see which score is moving and in which direction.

DRILL 01

"We're just looking today."

Who gains Profit from this line and why? What is the Intent?

ANSWER P −2 L −4 T Buyer Profit +6. This is a frame move. The buyer is establishing low-commitment positioning to reduce pressure on themselves. Intent is to prevent the agent from reading genuine interest, which would transfer Profit to the agent. Love drops slightly because it signals the buyer does not fully trust the agent yet. Tax drops because the buyer has reduced their own obligation.

undefined

DRILL 02

"I've been doing this for twenty-two years."

What score is this moving? For whom?

ANSWER P 0 L +6 T Agent Profit +8, Tax +6. This is a credential move. It moves Profit by establishing experience as leverage. But Tax builds simultaneously because the agent has now created an expectation of expertise they must consistently deliver. An agent who says this and then makes a basic error pays an outsized Love penalty.

undefined

DRILL 03

"The sellers are flexible on the closing date."

Score the move. Which character benefits most?

ANSWER P 0 L −8 T Buyer Profit +10, Tax −8. This is an intelligence share by the buyer's agent. It is one of the highest-value moves an agent can make in a showing because it creates Profit advantage for the buyer before any negotiation has started. Tax drops because the flexibility reduces timeline risk.

undefined

DRILL 04

"My husband really loves it but I'm not sure about the commute."

What is the scorer's priority after this line?

ANSWER P 0 L +8 T Buyer Profit −6, Tax +8. This is a split-decision signal. The husband's enthusiasm has just been offset by the wife's hesitation. Profit drops for the buyer because their decision has become conditional. Tax builds because the commute objection is now in play. The scorer's priority: address the commute objection specifically and immediately, not by dismissing it but by quantifying it.

undefined

DRILL 05

"I should have caught that issue earlier. That's on me."

What score moves most dramatically on this line?

ANSWER P +18 L +4 T Love +18. This is the most powerful single move available in any professional conversation. Ownership without excuse is the fastest Love-building move that exists. The person who says this loses nothing in Profit and gains almost everything in Love. Tax ticks up slightly because they have accepted responsibility, but the Love gain is so dominant that this is always the correct move.

undefined

DRILL 06

"Let me see what I can do."

Is this a Profit move, a Love move, or a Tax move? Whose?

ANSWER P −2 L +8 T Agent Tax +8. This is the most dangerous phrase in real estate. It is not a commitment and not a refusal. It creates Tax because it builds an implicit promise the agent may not be able to keep. Love drops because the client registers the non-commitment. Profit drops because the agent has stepped back from their expert position into an errand-runner position.

undefined

DRILL 07

"The only other offer came in at 560."

What just happened to the Buyer's score?

ANSWER P 0 L −10 T Buyer Profit +12, Tax −10. The agent just deployed a competing offer anchor. When a buyer hears there is another offer, Profit builds because they now have a reference point that replaces their imagined ceiling. Tax drops because the ambiguity about what to offer has been resolved — the floor has been set by the market.

undefined

DRILL 08

"I'm not going to pressure you — take whatever time you need."

What is happening to the agent's Profit?

ANSWER P +4 L 0 T Agent Profit −8, Love +4. This feels like a client-first move and emotionally it is. But strategically it is Profit surrender. The agent has removed urgency from a transaction where urgency is often the variable that creates decisions. Love builds because the client appreciates the lack of pressure. But the agent has now given up their strongest tool for moving a buyer off "we need to think about it."

undefined

pages.title: PART SIX
pages.html:
PART SIX

The Field Guide

One page per situation. What to watch. What it means. What to do.

THE SHOWING

What the Scorer Watches

THE BUYER SLOWS DOWN

WATCH FOR Client pace drops. They are spending more time in one room than the others.

IT MEANS The room they slow down in is the room they are deciding about. Everything else is evaluation. This room is negotiation.

YOUR MOVE Stop narrating the features. Let the silence run. Do not fill it. The buyer filling the silence is the most valuable information in the showing.

WE NEED TO THINK ABOUT IT

WATCH FOR The client is disengaging at the end of the showing.

IT MEANS Either the Love account is not high enough for them to trust the decision, or there is an unnamed Tax — a concern they have not said out loud. "Think about it" almost never means what it says.

YOUR MOVE Ask: "Is there something you need to know that you don't know yet?" Not "what are your concerns." What do you need to know. That question produces the real objection.

MY PARTNER HASN'T SEEN IT

WATCH FOR The client reveals a decision dependency mid-showing.

IT MEANS The deal cannot close without the partner. Everything from this point forward is staging for a conversation you are not in.

YOUR MOVE Get the partner scheduled before you leave the showing. Do not suggest it — make it easy. "Can we get them here Thursday evening? I'll make sure it works."

THE OFFER

What the Scorer Watches

THE BUYER ASKS WHAT YOU THINK THEY SHOULD OFFER

WATCH FOR The buyer has transferred the decision to you.

IT MEANS Their Love account for you is high. They trust you more than they trust their own analysis. This is the highest-influence moment in the transaction.

YOUR MOVE Give a specific number with a specific reason. Not a range. The buyer asking this question does not want options. They want conviction. Conviction is the offer.

THE SELLER COUNTER IS HIGHER THAN EXPECTED

WATCH FOR The counter came in near list despite a below-list offer.

IT MEANS The seller is anchored to a number that has emotional weight. The counter is not a negotiating position. It is a statement of value.

YOUR MOVE Do not counter the counter immediately. Ask the listing agent what timeline flexibility looks like. A seller anchored on price often has room in terms. Move the conversation from price to structure.

THE OTHER AGENT GOES SILENT AFTER THE OFFER

WATCH FOR You have submitted and the listing agent has stopped communicating.

IT MEANS Either another offer came in, the seller is deliberating, or the listing agent is managing a difficult principal. All three of these are different situations requiring different moves.

YOUR MOVE Call — do not text. A phone call signals urgency appropriately. Ask: "Is there anything my clients can provide that would help the decision?" That question reads as client-first and simultaneously gets you information.

THE NEGOTIATION

What the Scorer Watches

INSULTING OFFER LANGUAGE

WATCH FOR The other party uses emotional framing about the offer — insulting, low-ball, unrealistic.

IT MEANS They are negotiating from emotion rather than data. This is actually the weaker position. Emotional negotiators reveal more than strategic negotiators.

YOUR MOVE Do not match the emotion. Match the data. "Let me show you what the market supports and then we can look at the offer in that context." Data versus emotion — data wins if you hold the frame.

THE NEGOTIATION STALLS

WATCH FOR Multiple rounds of counter with no movement.

IT MEANS Both parties are protecting Profit at the cost of closing. The deal is Tax-negative for both — continued negotiation is costing both parties more than the gap between them.

YOUR MOVE Name the gap in dollars per day. "The gap between us is $8,000. Every week this doesn't close costs both parties roughly $1,200 in carrying costs, rate movement, and missed alternatives." Make the Tax of not closing visible.

THE CLOSING

What the Scorer Watches

COLD FEET BEFORE CLOSING

WATCH FOR The buyer's energy has dropped in the 72 hours before closing. Questions are increasing.

IT MEANS This is normal Tax response. The largest transaction of their life is about to become real. The questions are not about the house. They are about the decision.

YOUR MOVE Do not reassure. Validate. "This is the biggest purchase you have made. The feeling you have right now is appropriate. Here is what we have confirmed is true about this house and this transaction." Facts over encouragement.

THE LOAN OFFICER CALLS WITH A CONDITION

WATCH FOR An underwriting condition surfaces in the final week.

IT MEANS The buyer's Tax is about to spike. Their trust in the process is about to be tested. How this is handled in the next 60 minutes determines whether the deal closes.

YOUR MOVE Call the buyer before the loan officer does if at all possible. Frame it: "There is a condition on the file — here is exactly what it is, here is exactly what it requires, here is the timeline." Own the information. Do not let it arrive from a source you did not prepare them for.

The transaction does not end at closing.

The scores that ran through the deal — the Profit built, the Love earned, the Tax managed — those scores become the foundation of the next transaction. The buyer who closes with an agent they trust becomes the referral. The seller who felt heard becomes the repeat client. The loan officer who told the truth at the hard moment becomes the preferred partner.

The transaction is not a transaction. It is a ledger.

Every line you said, every moment you managed, every score you moved in the right direction — it accumulates. The scorer does not just close deals. The scorer builds a business that does not require starting over every quarter because the Love accounts are full and the Profit position is established and the Tax has been managed so well that clients do not come back with problems — they come back with people.

That is what Profit. Love. Tax. produces at full expression.

Not a single deal. A career.

About the Author

Craig Jones is the founder of the PLT Framework and the architect of the PLT Doctrine Series. He writes under the name Little Bunny. He built the framework from years of direct observation of how transactions actually work — what actually gets exchanged when two people negotiate, build trust, or walk away from a deal. The Scorer: Real Estate is the first in the career-specific Scorer series.
